outcome: Nothing has settled whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes since 26 January 2024. The window holds only finite additions of probable-prime indices, an unreviewed Zenodo counterexample to an index-pattern conjecture, an AI-assisted counterexample to a different question about Fibonacci numbers, a Lean statement of the open problem with its infinitude left as sorry, and a claimed proof whose page I could not read and whose date I could not establish.
problem_asks: (1) Whether the set of prime numbers that occur as Fibonacci numbers is infinite, i.e. whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes (primes equal to some F_n). That is the whole of the ask: a yes or no on infinitude, with no bound, count, or classification requested. Index form: infinitely many n with F_n prime. Since F_n is injective for n >= 2 and F_2 = 1 is not prime, counting values and counting indices gives the same answer.

events.what_happened: Jon Grantham and Andrew Granville, 'Fibonacci primes, primes of the form 2^n-k and beyond', arXiv:2307.07894. v1 was submitted 15 Jul 2023 and v3 comments say v1 was an earlier draft submitted inadvertently; v2 followed 18 Jul 2023 and v3 (9 Sep 2024) aligns with the journal version, J. Number Theory 261 (2024) 190-219. They adapt the polynomial prime-values heuristic to exponentially growing linear recurrences u_n and conjecture a dichotomy: either only finitely many u_n are prime, or there is c_u > 0 with roughly c_u log N primes u_n for n <= N. The paper proves nothing about Fibonacci primes and compares the conjecture with limited data. Journal date 20 Mar 2024 is from the sugaku.net aggregator, and the journal page was not opened.
events.revisions: v1 15 Jul 2023 (earlier draft, inadvertently submitted); v2 18 Jul 2023; v3 9 Sep 2024 (aligned with published version); journal J. Number Theory 261 (2024) 190-219.
events.delivers: Nothing proven about Fibonacci primes. A heuristic conjecture for the Fibonacci sequence and other linear recurrences: either finitely many prime terms, or about c_u log N prime terms with index up to N. The second branch is the infinite case, so the conjecture is consistent with either answer to the problem and predicts logarithmic growth of the count if infinite.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The heuristic is a prediction, not a theorem, and the question of infinitude is untouched.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in J. Number Theory 261 (2024) 190-219 per the sugaku.net aggregator (DOI 10.1016/j.jnt.2024.02.002, not opened). Referee reports not examined.

events.time_since_posted: about 3 years 3 months as of 11 Oct 2026 (v1)
events.direction: Does not claim infinitude or finiteness. Its conjecture is a dichotomy that predicts logarithmic growth in the count if the sequence of Fibonacci primes is infinite.

events.what_happened: Mark Broderius and John Greene, 'Lucas Sequences Containing Few Primes', Fibonacci Quarterly 59(2) (2021) 136-144. They give two families of Lucas sequences with only finitely many primes (one includes all Q that are perfect squares), and conjecture that every other Lucas sequence without obvious obstructions has infinitely many prime terms. Per the search snippet of the abstract, they state that it is beyond current techniques to prove that any Lucas sequence other than U_n(2,1) or U_n(-2,1) contains infinitely many primes. The Fibonacci sequence is U_n(1,-1) in standard parametrisation (my identification; the source text was not read).
events.delivers: Background only. No result on whether the Fibonacci sequence contains infinitely many primes. The two finiteness families do not include the Fibonacci parameters (P=1, Q=-1), so this event neither proves nor disproves infinitude, and it states that infinitude for almost all Lucas sequences is beyond current technique.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record for this area
checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (journal policy; referee reports not examined).

events.direction: Cuts toward finiteness for two special families and conjectures infinitude for the rest. States that the infinitude question is out of reach for nearly all Lucas sequences. Fibonacci is not one of the proven-finite families.

events.what_happened: Ismailescu, Jeon, Kim, Kwon and Lee, 'Shifting Lucas Sequences Away From Primes', Integers 25 (2025), article A42 (identified from a search snippet; the PDF at math.colgate.edu/~integers/z42/z42.pdf returned undecodable binary, so the text here is from the snippet). Theorem 1: U_n(3,-4) (0, 1, 3, 13, 51, 205, 819, ...) is composite for all n >= 4, so its only primes are 3 and 13. It also shifts Lucas sequences by a positive integer so that the shifted sequence has no primes, and strengthens a result of Jones. The paper's motivation is the finiteness side of the Broderius-Greene question.
events.delivers: One further Lucas sequence with finitely many primes, U_n(3,-4), and a shifting result. It is about Lucas sequences in general and does not concern the Fibonacci parameters, so it is a discounted event by scope.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published after refereeing (referee reports not examined).

events.directly_checkable: U_n(3,-4) can be checked by hand from the recurrence U_n = 3U_{n-1} + 4U_{n-2}; the snippet's first terms 0, 1, 3, 13, 51, 205, 819 are consistent with that recurrence.
events.direction: Cuts toward finiteness for the specific Lucas sequence U_n(3,-4). Says nothing about Fibonacci primes.
events.object: The Lucas sequence U_n(3,-4) with terms 0, 1, 3, 13, 51, 205, 819, ..., shown composite for all n >= 4 (an explicit family of examples; a proof that is not a counterexample to anything in the problem). The only primes are the terms 3 and 13.

events.what_happened: Attila Berczes, Lajos Hajdu, Florian Luca and Istvan Pink, 'On Fibonacci Numbers with Bounded Prime Gaps', preprint PDF in the University of Debrecen repository, dated 15 June 2025 in that record. The arXiv identifier was not found. Published as 'On members of Lucas sequences with bounded prime gaps', J. Number Theory 280 (2026) 897-917, DOI 10.1016/j.jnt.2025.09.005 (per the repository record). The paper studies Lucas-sequence terms whose prime factors have indices with bounded gaps; some results are conditional on widely believed conjectures; methods include Baker's method, the subspace theorem, and results of Stewart and of Murty-Wong. The paper notes that a prime F_n forces n = 4 or n prime. Per a search snippet, the authors say that proving infinitely many Fibonacci primes is almost certainly as hard as proving infinitely many Mersenne primes and that they do not know how to prove it. This snippet statement was not checked against the full text.
events.revisions: Preprint dated 15 Jun 2025 (repository copy); journal version J. Number Theory 280 (2026) 897-917 with a different title.
events.delivers: Partial results on a neighbouring question (bounded index gaps among prime factors of Lucas-sequence terms), some conditional. It does not prove or disprove infinitude of Fibonacci primes. Its statement that infinitude is out of reach is an expert opinion about difficulty, not a result.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record for number theory
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the revised paper in J. Number Theory 280 (2026) 897-917, per the Debrecen repository record (not opened). Referee reports not examined.

events.direction: Neither direction on the problem. It reports conditional and partial results about a neighbouring question and states that infinitude is hard.

events.what_happened: F_201107 (42,029 digits) is proved prime and is the largest proven Fibonacci prime in the lists checked. Wikipedia credits Maia Karpovich with the September 2023 proof. PrimePages lists it under discoverer E11, Sep 2023, method ECPP. This event predates the frozen revision and is included as background to the proven-record list. It is a computational instance and does not bear on infinitude.
events.delivers: One more proven Fibonacci prime, a computational instance. A finite addition to a list does not move the question of whether the list is infinite.
events.directly_checkable: The index 201107 can be re-tested with a primality test of F_201107; I did not run this.

events.what_happened: Five probable-prime indices added to OEIS A001605 (indices of prime Fibonacci numbers): a(52)-a(56) = 4740217, 6530879, 7789819, 10317107, 10367321, credited to Ryan Propper, added by Paul Bourdelais on 23 Aug 2024. OEIS also notes that some larger entries correspond only to probable primes, and that a(1)-a(37) are proven. The date is the OEIS addition date, the earliest dated public record found; the discovery date was not found.
events.revisions: OEIS A001605 later extended (a(57) added 2 Nov 2025, see next event).
events.delivers: Five further probable-prime indices. Probable primes are not proven primes, and the additions are finite, so they move nothing toward or against infinitude.
events.time_since_posted: about 2 years 2 months as of 11 Oct 2026
events.directly_checkable: Each index can be tested with a probable-prime test of F_n; I did not run any test.
events.doubts: The entries are probable primes. OEIS itself says larger entries may only correspond to probable primes.
events.direction: Not a claim about infinitude. Adds to the count of probable Fibonacci-prime indices.
people: Paul Bourdelais (OEIS editor who added the entries)

events.what_happened: a(57) = 11964299 added to OEIS A001605 by Hermann Stamm-Wilbrandt on 2 Nov 2025, credited to Ryan Propper and Serge Batalov. Wikipedia's infobox gives the largest known probable Fibonacci prime as F_11964299, found by Ryan Propper in June 2025. The June 2025 discovery date is from Wikipedia and I could not confirm it from a primary record, so I give the OEIS addition date as the dated public record.
events.revisions: Wikipedia states June 2025 for the find; OEIS records the addition on 2 Nov 2025.
events.delivers: One more probable-prime index, the largest in the lists checked. Probable only, and finite, so it moves nothing toward or against infinitude.
events.directly_checkable: Re-testable with a probable-prime test of F_11964299; not run.
events.doubts: Probable prime only. Discovery date rests on Wikipedia, not a primary record.

events.what_happened: Zenodo record 20569499, 'A Counterexample in Number Theory: Falsification of a Computational Conjecture', published 6 Jun 2026 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20569499, CC BY 4.0, PDF 'paper.pdf'). The creator field is 'SOVEREIGN Research Kernel', with no human author, affiliation or ORCID. The record states the conjecture: for every integer n >= 3, if F_n is prime then n is prime, and 2n+1 is prime or a semiprime. It says a counterexample was found computationally with witness = 13 and that 'This result was obtained by the SOVEREIGN autonomous research system.' Keywords include 'lean4' and 'formal verification', but I found no Lean artifact linked from the record. The PDF was not readable through the fetch tool. I checked by hand that 13 satisfies the falsifying conditions: F_13 = 233 is prime, 13 is prime, and 2*13+1 = 27 = 3^3 is neither prime nor a semiprime.
events.delivers: A counterexample to a conjecture about the indices of prime Fibonacci numbers (that they are prime and that 2n+1 is prime or semiprime). It does not touch whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes.
events.directly_checkable: The witness 13 can be checked by hand (done above). The record's own conjecture is also falsified at n = 4, since F_4 = 3 is prime and 4 is not; the record does not mention this, so 13 is not the least counterexample.
events.doubts: Unreviewed Zenodo deposit with no human author. The stated conjecture is already false at n = 4, which the record does not mention. The same record series includes other claims from search snippets that I could not verify (one reports a witness of 1000 for a perfect-power conjecture, which does not fit its own premise). The 'SOVEREIGN' system is named nowhere else in the sources I found.
events.direction: Cuts against the index-pattern conjecture it states, which is a different claim from the problem. It does not speak to infinitude either way.
events.object: A composite-index witness n = 13 for the stated index conjecture: F_13 = 233 is prime, 13 is prime, and 2n+1 = 27 is neither prime nor a semiprime. Explicit and checkable by hand. Not a counterexample to the problem.

systems.name: SOVEREIGN autonomous research system
systems.what_it_did: Obtained the counterexample (witness = 13) to the stated index-pattern conjecture, according to the record. Whether the system is an AI system is not stated in any readable source; the record calls it an autonomous research system and names no model.
systems.basis_quote: This result was obtained by the SOVEREIGN autonomous research system.

events.what_happened: Poo-Sung Park (Kyungnam University), 'The Fibonacci numbers are not an additive uniqueness set for multiplicative functions', arXiv:2609.08137, submitted 8 Sep 2026 (single version). The paper answers Spiro's 1992 question negatively: a multiplicative function satisfying f(F_n + F_m) = f(F_n) + f(F_m) need not be the identity. The smallest example comes from F_31 = 557 * 2417. The comments field reads '7 pages, AI-assisted'. The abstract says 'We also describe the AI-assisted search that led to the construction and provide a reproducible certificate checker.' Section 6, 'AI-assisted discovery and verification', says: 'The initial example was found in September 2026 in an interactive ChatGPT session using OpenAI GPT-6 Astra.' The paper does not mention Fibonacci primes; its objects are Fibonacci numbers and their prime factors.
events.delivers: A negative answer to an additive-uniqueness question about multiplicative functions on Fibonacci numbers, with an explicit example from F_31. It concerns functional equations on F_n, not prime Fibonacci numbers, so it is a different question.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. Nothing here counts or constrains Fibonacci primes.
events.directly_checkable: The counterexample F_31 = 557 * 2417 and the defining condition can be checked by hand or with a short script; I did not check it.
events.direction: Negative answer to Spiro's additive-uniqueness question for Fibonacci numbers. Says nothing about whether Fibonacci primes are infinite.
events.object: A multiplicative function f with f(F_n + F_m) = f(F_n) + f(F_m) that is not the identity; the smallest example is built from the factorisation F_31 = 557 * 2417 and is given with a prime-signature construction and a certificate checker. Explicit, not a non-constructive existence proof.

systems.name: OpenAI GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: In the authors' words: 'It proposed replacing the value at one prime by the other prime' and 'It designed and ran an exact-integer search'; the authors also say 'recognized that multiplicativity is preserved by the indicator formula'. They say the pair (557, 2417) from F_31 was the first successful pair retained in this search. The authors add: 'The language model's output was therefore a discovery aid, not a substitute for verification.' The search produced the counterexample, so the contribution is load-bearing for this paper, though not for the Fibonacci-prime question.
systems.basis_quote: The initial example was found in September 2026 in an interactive ChatGPT session using OpenAI GPT-6 Astra.

events.what_happened: A ResearchGate publication titled 'There are Infinitely Many Fibonacci Primes' (URL publication id 343830174) that asserts a proof of infinitude. The ResearchGate page returned HTTP 403 and I could not read its abstract, date, author list, or body. A search summary attributed it to 'Fengsui Liu', but that name comes only from the search summary and is not confirmed by the page. A search for the exact title returned no other copy and no reference to it. I could not establish any date, so the date field is null.
events.delivers: Claimed proof of infinitude. Nothing about its mathematics was readable, so what it delivers cannot be stated beyond its title.
events.remains: Unknown. If the claim held, it would settle all of problem_asks; I have no evidence that it does.
events.doubts: Only a name-level link: a primepuzzles.net page (search result, not opened) records a Fengsui Liu who in 2001 sent an argument he believed proved the prime k-tuple conjecture, and states that the argument's validity is not established. Whether that is the same author is not confirmed. No mathematician's engagement with the ResearchGate claim was found, and no source treats infinitude of Fibonacci primes as settled.
events.direction: Claims infinitude, which would cut toward the infinite side. Unverified and unreadable.
people: Fengsui Liu (name from a search summary only; not confirmed on the page)

events.what_happened: Lenny Jones, 'Fibonacci Variations of a Conjecture of Polignac', Integers 12 (2012). Proves that there are infinitely many positive integers that cannot be written as F_n + p or F_n - p with p prime. Follow-ups: Ismailescu and Shim, Integers 14 (2014); Bresz, Jones, Lamarche and Markovich, Integers 16 (2016), on 2n + F_n +/- p. Identified from search snippets; the papers were not opened.
events.delivers: Results on which integers are representable as a Fibonacci number plus or minus a prime. This is a different question: it concerns integers represented by Fibonacci-plus-prime expressions, not whether Fibonacci numbers are prime.
events.direction: Not applicable to the problem; a Polignac-type variant that is a neighbouring question.

events.what_happened: B. B. Sharpe, 'A Fibonacci-Prime Number Relation', Fibonacci Quarterly 2(4), on sums and differences of Fibonacci numbers being prime. Per a search summary: if i + j is prime then F_i + F_j is prime for at least one i (sum version), and a difference version with i + j prime and greater than 3. The year 1964 is inferred from the volume number, since the scanned PDF had no legible text. Not opened. I found no proof or disproof of either version in my searches.
events.delivers: Conjectures about sums and differences of Fibonacci numbers being prime. Not a result, and about a different question from the infinitude of Fibonacci primes.
events.direction: Not applicable; these are conjectures about different expressions.

events.what_happened: A 2005 paper by Cai, Chen and Zhang, titled 'Perfect Numbers and Fibonacci Primes (I)', is reported in a search snippet as linking Fibonacci primes to the twin prime conjecture: the twin prime conjecture holds if and only if sigma_2(n) - n^2 = 2n + 5 has infinitely many solutions, and for (A,B) = (L_2m, F_2m^2 - 1) the solutions are n = F_2k+1 F_2k+2m+1 with both factors Fibonacci primes, apart from finitely many exceptions. The source I was given (arXiv math/0510171) resolves to an unrelated twin-prime paper by Du and Du, so I could not locate this paper and could not verify the snippet. Recorded so the gap is visible.
events.delivers: If the snippet is accurate: a conditional equivalence to the twin prime conjecture and a description of certain perfect-number solutions in terms of Fibonacci primes. Neither gives infinitude of Fibonacci primes, and the equivalence is to a different problem.
events.doubts: Could not verify: the arXiv identifier given in a search result resolves to a different paper.
events.direction: Not applicable to infinitude. Any equivalence is to the twin prime conjecture.

events.what_happened: Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, file FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/FibonacciPrimes.lean (copyright 2025). It states the infinitude problem in Lean in two phrasings: fib_primes_infinite (the set of n that are Fibonacci numbers and prime is infinite) and fib_primes_infinite.variant (the set of n with n.fib prime is infinite). Both carry sorry and are tagged 'research open'. The theorem indices_infinite_iff_fib_primes_infinite, showing the two phrasings are equivalent, is fully proved with no sorry. The file's docstring describes the statement as the main open conjecture. The commit date was not visible.
events.delivers: A formal statement of the open problem with the infinitude left unproved, plus a proof that the two phrasings are equivalent. It establishes nothing about whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes.
events.direction: Not applicable to truth. The formal statement is the open problem itself, with the infinitude unproved.
people: Google DeepMind formal-conjectures contributors (individual authors not identified in the file header I read)

disputes.summary: Discoverer of the proven record F_201107 (Sept 2023): Wikipedia credits Maia Karpovich; PrimePages lists discoverer E11 with method ECPP. These may be the same person under different handles, which I did not establish.

Discovery date of the probable prime F_11964299: Wikipedia says found by Ryan Propper in June 2025; the OEIS entry records its addition on 2 Nov 2025 with Propper and Batalov credited. The June 2025 date has no primary source in my record.

The PrimePages Fibonacci page's running text lists 104911, 130021, 148091 and 201107 as probable, but its table marks the same indices ECPP (proven) and Wikipedia's proven list includes them. I follow Wikipedia's proven/probable split and the table's ECPP marks; the text appears out of date.

summary: Searched 39 queries and fetched about 30 pages, of which roughly 20 returned readable text; the rest are listed in incomplete. Wikipedia's Fibonacci prime article, read directly, says it is not known whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes. It lists 37 proven indices (largest proven F_201107, 42,029 digits, Sept 2023) and 20 probable indices (largest F_11964299, reported June 2025 per Wikipedia). No source I could read proves or refutes infinitude, and I found no refereed or expert engagement with any proof attempt. The Grantham-Granville heuristic (arXiv July 2023, J. Number Theory 2024) predicts either finitely many or roughly c_u log N Fibonacci primes up to N; Broderius and Greene (2021) state that infinitude is beyond current technique for every Lucas sequence except U_n(2,1) and U_n(-2,1), and Fibonacci is not in their finite-prime families; Berczes, Hajdu, Luca and Pink (preprint June 2025) say proving infinitude is almost certainly as hard as for Mersenne primes (the sentence comes from a search snippet). Inside the window the events are: (i) five probable-prime indices added to OEIS A001605 on 23 Aug 2024, and a(57) = 11964299 added 2 Nov 2025 (Propper, Batalov); these are finite additions of probable primes and move nothing on infinitude. I weighed whether they are 'newly confirmed instances growing' under the scope test. They are instances of the same existential question, but finitely many, so they do not bear on 'infinitely many'. (ii) A Zenodo record dated 6 June 2026 by 'SOVEREIGN Research Kernel' claims a counterexample to a conjecture on indices (F_n prime implies n prime and 2n+1 prime or semiprime) with witness 13; I verified 13 by hand, but the same conjecture is already falsified at n = 4 (F_4 = 3), which the record omits. It concerns indices, not infinitude; the record has no human author, and whether the 'SOVEREIGN autonomous research system' is an AI system is not stated anywhere readable. (iii) arXiv:2609.08137 (Poo-Sung Park, 8 Sep 2026) answers Spiro's additive-uniqueness question for multiplicative functions on Fibonacci numbers, with an explicit example from F_31 = 557 * 2417, and credits 'OpenAI GPT-6 Astra' with proposing the key structural step and running the search that produced the example. This is the clearest AI-involved event in the record, and it is discounted by scope: it concerns Fibonacci numbers, not Fibonacci primes, and the paper never mentions Fibonacci primes. (iv) DeepMind's formal-conjectures file states the infinitude problem in Lean with the infinitude as sorry, and proves the two phrasings equivalent; this is a benchmark formalisation, not progress. (v) A ResearchGate publication 'There are Infinitely Many Fibonacci Primes' (publication id 343830174) claims a proof of infinitude. The page returned HTTP 403, I found no date, and the author name appears only in a search summary. This is the one item that, if real and dated in the window, would bear directly on the question, and it is the largest gap in this record. Pre-window neighbours (Jones 2012 on F_n +/- p; Sharpe's 1964 sum and difference conjectures; a 2005 Cai-Chen-Zhang claim I could not locate) are recorded as different questions. Also checked: the OpenAI openai/math release (press figure 722 manuscripts; README says 719 manuscripts in 372 families, produced by 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model' with roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro compute each). Its readable CONTENTS.md chunks contain no Fibonacci-prime manuscript, but the read was partial (see incomplete). Gemini and Claude search hits concern other problems (Erdos problems, the zeta-function zero bound, Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean).
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading this differently is the ResearchGate claim: if it is a valid proof of infinitude first written in the window, the problem is settled and the record's status would change entirely; I cannot exclude that because the page was unreadable and its date unknown. A second reading treats the 2024-2025 probable-prime additions and the 2026 counterexamples as progress on the problem; that fails the scope test, because finite additions and counterexamples to index patterns or to Fibonacci-number analogues do not move 'infinitely many'.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A readable copy of the ResearchGate PDF (publication 343830174) with its date, author and any comments, and any refereed venue or expert check of it. (2) A referee-accepted or Lean-verified proof of infinitude, which would settle the problem. (3) For the SOVEREIGN record: the PDF text, any linked code or Lean artifact, a statement of whether the system is an AI system, and a note of the n = 4 case. (4) For Park: a copy of the paper's full text to confirm the quoted AI sentences word for word, since they came through a summarising fetch. (5) For the Bérczes et al. and Grantham-Granville statements: the full texts, to confirm the expert statements and the heuristic's wording. (6) The OEIS and PrimePages discovery dates for the 2024-2025 probable primes, to replace the addition dates with discovery dates.
